summary:
Niue sets its own criminal law on sexual conduct. Consensual male homosexual activity is no longer an offence: the Niue Assembly passed the Niue (Sexual Offences) Amendment Act in May 2024, in force from June 2024 (enacted 5 June 2024), removing buggery, attempted buggery and indecent assault on males from the Criminal Law Code. The age of consent was equalised in May 2011.

Before that repeal, sections 43 and 44 of the Criminal Law Code criminalised male homosexual conduct: consensual sodomy carried up to ten years' imprisonment and indecency between males up to five years, with attempted buggery and indecent assault on males falling under the same provisions. The offences were inherited from New Zealand through the 1901 annexation, retained when Niue took self-government in 1974, and left in place by New Zealand's 1986 decriminalisation, which amended New Zealand law only.

Marriage and partner recognition are closed to couples the law reads as same-sex. Same-sex unions are not recognised in Niue even though they are recognised in New Zealand, and section 6 of the Family Relationships Act 2022 expressly prohibits same-sex marriage. Couples and households headed by such couples are not eligible for the legal protections available to opposite-sex married couples. A trans visitor whose relationship would be classified locally as same-sex has no route to recognition or to the protections attached to marriage.

A 2015 UN Free & Equal information sheet on the Pacific records the fakafifine of Niue among the region's pre-colonial gender identities, which it describes as important parts of the region's cultural heritage.
tangentialFactors:
Niue is in free association with New Zealand, which recognises same-sex unions. That recognition does not extend to Niue, and Niuean law governs marriage and family relationships there.

The age of majority under the Niue Act 1966 (Part 21, Marriage of Minors) is 21 for men and 19 for women, an asymmetry that remains on the books. The provision sits in the part of the Act dealing with marriage of minors and is not specific to trans people.
localsOnly:
Residents in relationships the law reads as same-sex cannot marry: section 6 of the Family Relationships Act 2022 prohibits same-sex marriage, and same-sex unions are not recognised. Households headed by such couples are not eligible for the legal protections that attach to opposite-sex marriage.

The 2024 repeal removed from Niuean law the offences that had applied to residents since before self-government. Consensual sodomy, which carried up to ten years, and indecency between males, which carried up to five years, are no longer offences.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory records enforcement practice under the repealed sections, the number of prosecutions brought under them, or police and court treatment of trans and gender-nonconforming people in Niue.

No source records Niue's rules on gender markers or identity documents, or access to transition-related healthcare.

No source records hate-crime or anti-discrimination protection covering gender identity, or its enforcement.

The 2015 UN Free & Equal information sheet predates the 2024 repeal and does not describe current conditions.

The age of majority figures rest on a third-party compilation of the Niue Act 1966 rather than an official text in this inventory.
